rv.q: What makes Golyak’s production really roar into flame is the astonishing magnetism of his performers...

Golyak and his gifted collaborators sail right down the middle, bringing us something that is two parts slapstick to one part tragedy, seasoned with just enough whimsy and terror to bleed tension off in a laugh with one hand while creating genuine suspense with the other.
Golyak’s production achieves delicate balances between timeliness and timelessness, hilarity and horror, and the result is an astonishing piece of work.
Muscular performances and jaw-dropping design come together seamlessly for an evening of theater that will linger in my memory for a long time.

Golyak and his Boston-based Arlekin Players have demonstrated a level of theatrical imagination and social conscience – in such works as “Our Class,” “Witness,” and their various experimental versions of The Cherry Orchard – to make me eager to see anything they do, no matter the obstacles.
It has the form of the great postwar absurdist works but not the spark of mad genius.
Everything about this production is wonderful and it will have you standing and cheering come curtain call.
Rarely does one experience a theatrical explosion like Delirium – all happening in the tiny second-floor Space at Irondale in Brooklyn.

What Delirium gets right is capturing the lengths to which people will go to normalize the extreme, the rationalizations of people who've grown accustomed to untenable situations — whether domestic or political.

Igor Golyak’s Delirium , an adaptation of Ionesco’s 1962 play Délire à deux ( Frenzy for Two ), captures this signature blend of slapstick domestic squabbling while highlighting the human penchant for destruction and barbarity.
Golyak and this exceptional company bring all of that to the stage in a production that deserves to be seen.
Igor Golyak is one of the most exciting, inventive, and innovative directors working today, and he proves it yet again with the absolutely mind-blowing Delirium.

cn.t: Critics hail Golyak's electrifying adaptation of Ionesco's obscure absurdist play as brilliant and thrilling, praising the exceptional chemistry between exiled Russian actors Khamatova and Burkovskiy, though some find the devotion to nonsense exhausting.

vr.q: I enjoyed the clever ideas... but it just wasn't working all together for me.
